summary: A US jury convicts Huawei, a Huawei-chip data centre starts selling AI computing abroad, universities hand out free AI tokens, and regulators weigh airline mergers.
body: A US federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei and three affiliates guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets, while acquitting it of racketeering conspiracy.[^1] Huawei says it will appeal. Chinese officials have long called the case "economic bullying" that uses national security as a pretext.[^2] The verdict lands as Huawei's Ascend chips become China's main alternative to Nvidia.[^1]

Those chips now power China's first AI computing cluster built for foreign customers, at a China Telecom undersea-cable station in Shantou, Guangdong. Reported at about $150 million, it sells "tokens", the units AI models use to process text, to users abroad.[^3] At home, tokens are becoming an everyday perk. The University of Science and Technology of China gives every student and teacher 100 million free tokens a day, and Tongji University in Shanghai 100 million a week, for models such as DeepSeek and Qwen.[^4] Banks, phone companies and even cafés bundle them with credit cards, phone plans and coffee.[^6]

China's aviation regulator is weighing mergers of smaller loss-making airlines from next year, the South China Morning Post reports; Reuters could not verify it.[^5] The three biggest carriers had much weaker third-quarter results, citing jet fuel costs and low domestic fares. Fewer airlines could mean fewer cheap tickets over time.[^5]
differences: US prosecutors describe company-wide fraud and theft; Huawei blames a few fired employees and will appeal; Beijing calls the case political.[^1][^2]
